extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners and patent practitioners (patent prosecution)
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating patent subject-matter eligibility under the 2019 USPTO Patent Eligibility Guidance (PEG), with emphasis on life-sciences examples (nature-based products, mixtures, and treatment/process claims) and how to apply Steps 1, 2A (two prongs), and 2B.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim interpretation (broadest reasonable interpretation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the broadest reasonable interpretation, the terms of the claim are presumed to have their plain meaning consistent with the specification as it would be interpreted by one of ordinary skill in the art. MPEP 2111.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No limitations can be disregarded; a wherein clause still may have patentable weight. Use the specification to determine what the claim language encompasses when applying eligibility analyses (e.g., whether a functional wherein clause imposes structural limitation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 1 — Statutory category evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: This part of the eligibility analysis evaluates whether the claim falls within any statutory category. MPEP 2106.03.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify if the claim is to a process, composition of matter, machine, or manufacture. It is sufficient that the claim falls into at least one statutory category (e.g., a protein is a composition of matter; a container is a manufacture).

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2A Prong One — Does the claim recite a judicial exception?
rubrics_metrics.description: This part of the eligibility analysis evaluates whether the claim recites a judicial exception (e.g., law of nature, natural phenomenon, product of nature, abstract idea).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine whether elements of the claim 'set forth' or 'describe' an exception. For nature-based product limitations, this raises the question of whether the product is a product-of-nature exception and therefore whether a markedly different characteristics analysis applies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Markedly Different Characteristics analysis for nature-based products
rubrics_metrics.description: The markedly different characteristics analysis is performed by comparing the nature-based product limitation in the claim to its naturally occurring counterpart to determine if it has markedly different characteristics from the counterpart. MPEP 2106.04(c)(II).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare structure, function, and other characteristics. If there are no differences in structure, function, or other characteristics, the claimed nature-based product may be a product-of-nature exception (ineligible). If the claimed product has changed functional properties or other marked differences, it is not a product-of-nature exception (not a judicial exception). It is not necessary that the claim explicitly recite the different characteristic so long as the broadest reasonable interpretation of the claim reflects it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Process claims: general rule for nature-based product limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: For a process claim, the general rule is that the claim is not subject to the markedly different analysis for nature-based products used in the process. MPEP 2106.04(c)(I)(C).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exception exists where a process claim is drafted such that it is no different in substance than a product claim; only then might the markedly different analysis be applied. Otherwise, do not treat nature-based product limitations in process claims as automatically 'reciting' products of nature for eligibility analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2A Prong Two — Integration into a practical application
rubrics_metrics.description: This part of the eligibility analysis evaluates whether the claim as a whole integrates the recited judicial exception into a practical application of the exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perform (a) identification of additional elements beyond the judicial exception and (b) evaluation of those additional elements individually and in combination to determine whether the claim integrates the exception into a practical application. Consider 'particular machine' and 'other meaningful limitations' as ways that integration may be shown. Exclude, at this prong, consideration of whether an additional element is well-understood, routine, or conventional (2019 PEG Section III(A)(2)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Particular-machine consideration (three-factor test)
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether a recited machine is a 'particular machine' using the three factors set forth in MPEP 2106.05(b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factors include whether the machine is recited at a high level of generality or as a particular machine with specific components, and whether the machine is an integral part of the claim (more than a field-of-use or insignificant limitation). If it is a particular machine that applies or uses the exception in a meaningful way, it can integrate the exception into a practical application (example: delivery device with reservoir, valve, needle assembly).

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2B — Whether claim amounts to 'significantly more' (inventive concept)
rubrics_metrics.description: This part of the eligibility analysis evaluates whether the claim as a whole amounts to significantly more than the recited exception, i.e., whether any additional element, or combination of additional elements, adds an inventive concept to the claim. MPEP 2106.05.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether additional elements are sufficient to transform the claim into eligible subject matter. Mere instructions to apply an exception (e.g., a generic container or 'apply it') cannot provide an inventive concept. Cite MPEP 2106.05 and case law as appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mixtures and multi-component nature-based products — resultant combination analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: When the claim is to a nature-based product produced by combining multiple components, the markedly different characteristics analysis should be applied to the resultant nature-based combination rather than its component parts. MPEP 2106.04(c)(I)(A).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the components do not occur together in nature and the claimed combination exhibits a changed functional property (e.g., changed glycemic control profile), the combination may have markedly different characteristics and therefore not be a product-of-nature exception. Compare the resultant mixture to its natural counterpart(s) or components as appropriate (examples: denveric acid + protamine resulting in different onset/ duration).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mere instructions to apply an exception — anti-pattern
rubrics_metrics.description: Mere instructions to apply an exception (for example, adding a generic 'container' or the words 'apply it') cannot provide an inventive concept and thus do not make a claim 'significantly more.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When additional limitations are generic or amount to nothing more than 'apply it,' the claim fails Step 2B. Examiners should explain why a limitation is merely an instruction to apply the exception and may cite MPEP 2106.05(f) and relevant case law (e.g., Roslin, Myriad) in the rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusion of conventionality at Step 2A Prong Two
rubrics_metrics.description: When evaluating integration into a practical application at Step 2A Prong Two, exclude consideration of whether a limitation is well-understood, routine, or conventional. (2019 PEG Section III(A)(2), 84 Fed. Reg. at 55).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely on the conventionality or routine nature of an additional element to decide whether it integrates the judicial exception into a practical application under Step 2A Prong Two. Conventionality may be relevant later at Step 2B (inventive concept) or in other substantive rejections (e.g., obviousness).

rubrics_metrics.name: Practice note — compact prosecution and other statutory requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Although a claim may be eligible under subject-matter eligibility analysis, it may be unpatentable for other reasons; examiners should practice compact prosecution by examining each claim for compliance with every statutory requirement for patentability in the initial review of the application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate prior art anticipation and obviousness (including applicant-admitted prior art), indefiniteness, written description, and whether functional genus claims are supported by correlation between structure and function. Cite MPEP 2129(I), 2173.05(g), 2163(II)(A)(3)(a) as relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practice note — Streamlined analysis (Pathway A) vs Full analysis (Pathway B)
rubrics_metrics.description: For examination efficiency, examiners may use a streamlined eligibility analysis (Pathway A) when the eligibility of the claim is self-evident; if the claim is a 'close call,' perform a full analysis (Pathway B). MPEP 2106.06.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of claims suitable for Pathway A include claims that clearly are not attempts to tie up a natural product (e.g., wearable delivery device with detailed components). If the eligibility outcome is not self-evident, perform the full Step 2A/2B analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection drafting guidance for nature-based product claims
rubrics_metrics.description: A rejection should identify the exception by pointing to the nature-based product in the claim (e.g., denveric acid) and explain why it is a product-of-nature exception, and explain why the claim as a whole does not integrate the exception into a practical application or amount to significantly more than the exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain the marked-difference comparison and why additional limitations are insufficient (e.g., generic container). If helpful, cite court decisions (e.g., Roslin, Myriad, Funk Brothers) and MPEP sections (e.g., 2106.05(f)) to support the reasoning.
